claim: Marmosets were engaged in a foraging task where they made saccades to visual targets to accumulate food, then harvested by licking.
source: we engaged marmosets in a foraging task in which on each trial they decided whether to work by making saccades to visual targets, thus accumulating food, or to harvest by licking what they had earned.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: The effort cost of harvest was varied by moving the food tube with respect to the mouth.
source: We varied the effort cost of harvest by moving the food tube with respect to the mouth.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental manipulation performed.

claim: In response to increased effort cost of harvest, marmosets extended their work duration.
source: Indeed, in response to an increased effort cost of harvest, marmosets extended their work duration, but slowed their movements.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations from the study.

claim: In response to increased effort cost of harvest, marmosets slowed their movements.
source: Indeed, in response to an increased effort cost of harvest, marmosets extended their work duration, but slowed their movements.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations from the study.

claim: Changes in decisions and movements coincided with changes in pupil size.
source: These changes in decisions and movements coincided with changes in pupil size.
evidence: The manuscript reports observed correlations in the experimental data.

claim: As the effort cost of harvest declined, work duration decreased.
source: As the effort cost of harvest declined, work duration decreased, the pupils dilated, and the vigor of licks and saccades increased.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations from the study.

claim: As the effort cost of harvest declined, the pupils dilated.
source: As the effort cost of harvest declined, work duration decreased, the pupils dilated, and the vigor of licks and saccades increased.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations from the study.

claim: As the effort cost of harvest declined, the vigor of licks and saccades increased.
source: As the effort cost of harvest declined, work duration decreased, the pupils dilated, and the vigor of licks and saccades increased.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations from the study.

claim: When acquisition of reward became effortful, the pupils constricted.
source: Thus, when acquisition of reward became effortful, the pupils constricted, the decisions exhibited delayed gratification, and the movements displayed reduced vigor.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations from the study.

claim: When acquisition of reward became effortful, the decisions exhibited delayed gratification.
source: Thus, when acquisition of reward became effortful, the pupils constricted, the decisions exhibited delayed gratification, and the movements displayed reduced vigor.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations from the study.

claim: When acquisition of reward became effortful, the movements displayed reduced vigor.
source: Thus, when acquisition of reward became effortful, the pupils constricted, the decisions exhibited delayed gratification, and the movements displayed reduced vigor.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations from the study.

claim: During foraging, animals work to locate a food cache and then spend effort harvesting what they have found.
source: During foraging, animals work to locate a food cache and then spend effort harvesting what they have found.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal foraging behavior based on established knowledge.

claim: Animals' foraging decisions appear to maximize the sum of rewards acquired, minus efforts expended, divided by time, termed the capture rate.
source: As they forage, their decisions appear to maximize a measure that is relevant to fitness: the sum of rewards acquired, minus efforts expended, divided by time, termed the capture rate (Charnov, 1976; Cowie, 1977; Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A crow will spend effort extracting a clam from a sandy beach, but if the clam is small, it will abandon it because the additional time and effort required to extract the small reward can be better spent finding a bigger prize.
source: For example, a crow will spend effort extracting a clam from a sandy beach, but if the clam is small, it will abandon it because the additional time and effort required to extract the small reward – dropping it repeatedly from a height onto rocks – can be better spent finding a bigger prize (Richardson and Verbeek, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Reward expectation affects movements: we not only prefer the less effortful option, we also move vigorously to obtain it.
source: Intriguingly, reward expectation not only affects decisions, it also affects movements: we not only prefer the less effortful option, we also move vigorously to obtain it (Yoon et al., 2020; Korbisch et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Movements require expenditure of time and energy, which discount the value of the promised reward.
source: This modulation of movement vigor can be justified if we consider that movements require expenditure of time and energy, which discount the value of the promised reward (Shadmehr et al., 2010; Shadmehr et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There should exist a mechanism to coordinate control of decisions with control of movements so that both contribute to maximizing fitness.
source: Thus, from a theoretical perspective, there should exist a mechanism to coordinate control of decisions with control of movements so that both contribute to maximizing fitness (Yoon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by a citation.

claim: Theory predicted that in order to maximize the capture rate, harvest should commence only when there was sufficient reward accumulated to justify the effort required for its extraction.
source: Theory predicted that in order to maximize the capture rate, harvest should commence only when there was sufficient reward accumulated to justify the effort required for its extraction.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The subjects chose to work and stockpile food, and only then initiated their harvest.
source: Indeed, the subjects chose to work and stockpile food, and only then initiated their harvest.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations from the study.

claim: As the effort cost increased, the subjects should choose to work more trials, thus delaying their harvest so to stow more food, but reduce their movement vigor, thus saving energy.
source: The theory made two interesting predictions: as the effort cost increased, the subjects should choose to work more trials, thus delaying their harvest so to stow more food, but reduce their movement vigor, thus saving energy.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: When marmosets encountered an increased effort cost, they extended their work period, stockpiling food, but reduced their vigor, slowing their saccades during the work period, and slowing their licks during the harvest period.
source: Indeed, when marmosets encountered an increased effort cost, they extended their work period, stockpiling food, but reduced their vigor, slowing their saccades during the work period, and slowing their licks during the harvest period.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations from the study.

claim: During the work and the harvest periods, momentary changes in pupil size closely tracked the changes in vigor.
source: During the work and the harvest periods, momentary changes in pupil size closely tracked the changes in vigor: pupil dilation accompanied increases in vigor, while pupil constriction accompanied decreases in vigor.
evidence: The manuscript reports observed correlations in the experimental data.

claim: Pupil dilation accompanied increases in vigor, while pupil constriction accompanied decreases in vigor.
source: During the work and the harvest periods, momentary changes in pupil size closely tracked the changes in vigor: pupil dilation accompanied increases in vigor, while pupil constriction accompanied decreases in vigor.
evidence: The manuscript reports observed correlations in the experimental data.

claim: The relationship between pupil size and vigor was true regardless of whether the movement that was being performed was a saccade or a lick.
source: Remarkably, this was true regardless of whether the movement that was being performed was a saccade or a lick.
evidence: The manuscript reports observed correlations in the experimental data.

claim: In response to the increased effort cost, the pupils exhibited a global change, constricting during both the work and the harvest periods.
source: Moreover, in response to the increased effort cost, the pupils exhibited a global change, constricting during both the work and the harvest periods.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations from the study.

claim: Changes in pupil size can be viewed as a proxy for activity in the brainstem noradrenergic circuits.
source: If we view the changes in pupil size as a proxy for activity in the brainstem noradrenergic circuits (Joshi and Gold, 2020), our results suggest that as these circuits respond to effort costs (Bornert and Bouret, 2021), they alter computations in the brain regions that control decisions, delaying gratification and encouraging work, and the brain regions that control movements, promoting sloth and conserving energy.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: As brainstem noradrenergic circuits respond to effort costs, they alter computations in the brain regions that control decisions, delaying gratification and encouraging work, and the brain regions that control movements, promoting sloth and conserving energy.
source: If we view the changes in pupil size as a proxy for activity in the brainstem noradrenergic circuits (Joshi and Gold, 2020), our results suggest that as these circuits respond to effort costs (Bornert and Bouret, 2021), they alter computations in the brain regions that control decisions, delaying gratification and encouraging work, and the brain regions that control movements, promoting sloth and conserving energy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on prior research.

claim: Over the course of 2.5 years, 56 sessions were recorded in subject M (29 months) and 56 sessions in subject R (23 months).
source: Over the course of 2.5 y, we recorded 56 sessions in subject M (29 mo) and 56 sessions in subject R (23 mo).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental data collection.

claim: A typical work period lasted about 10 seconds.
source: A typical work period lasted about 10 s, during which the subjects attempted ~8 trials and succeeded in 4–5 trials (Figure 1D) (a successful trial was when all three saccades were within 1.25o of the center of each target).
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from the experimental data and references Figure 1D.

claim: During a typical work period, the subjects attempted approximately 8 trials and succeeded in 4-5 trials.
source: A typical work period lasted about 10 s, during which the subjects attempted ~8 trials and succeeded in 4–5 trials (Figure 1D) (a successful trial was when all three saccades were within 1.25o of the center of each target).
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from the experimental data and references Figure 1D.

claim: A successful trial was when all three saccades were within 1.25 degrees of the center of each target.
source: A typical work period lasted about 10 s, during which the subjects attempted ~8 trials and succeeded in 4–5 trials (Figure 1D) (a successful trial was when all three saccades were within 1.25o of the center of each target).
evidence: The manuscript defines the criterion for a successful trial.

claim: The work period ended when the subject decided to stop tracking the targets and instead initiated harvest, which lasted about 6 seconds, resulting in 16-18 licks.
source: The work period ended when the subject decided to stop tracking the targets and instead initiated harvest, which lasted about 6 s, resulting in 16–18 licks.
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from the experimental data.

claim: Subject M completed an average of 909.5 ± 61 successful trials per session, producing an average of 241 ± 13.9 work-harvest pairs.
source: Subject M completed an average of 909.5 ± 61 successful trials per session (mean ± SEM), producing an average of 241 ± 13.9 work-harvest pairs, and subject R completed an average of 1431 ± 65 successful trials, producing an average of 263 ± 8.9 work-harvest pairs.
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from the experimental data.

claim: Subject R completed an average of 1431 ± 65 successful trials per session, producing an average of 263 ± 8.9 work-harvest pairs.
source: Subject M completed an average of 909.5 ± 61 successful trials per session (mean ± SEM), producing an average of 241 ± 13.9 work-harvest pairs, and subject R completed an average of 1431 ± 65 successful trials, producing an average of 263 ± 8.9 work-harvest pairs.
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from the experimental data.

claim: Food was delivered via either the left or the right tube for 50-300 consecutive trials and then switched tubes.
source: We delivered food via either the left or the right tube for 50–300 consecutive trials and then switched tubes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The tube was 4.4 mm in diameter.
source: The licks required precision because the tube was just large enough (4.4 mm diameter) to allow the tongue to penetrate.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental apparatus.

claim: About 30% of the reward-seeking licks were successful and contacted food.
source: As a result, about 30% of the reward-seeking licks were successful and contacted food (30 ± 1.6% for subject M, 28 ± 2.5% for subject R), as shown in Animation 1.
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from the experimental data and references Animation 1.

claim: For subject M, 30 ± 1.6% of reward-seeking licks were successful.
source: As a result, about 30% of the reward-seeking licks were successful and contacted food (30 ± 1.6% for subject M, 28 ± 2.5% for subject R), as shown in Animation 1.
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from the experimental data.

claim: For subject R, 28 ± 2.5% of reward-seeking licks were successful.
source: As a result, about 30% of the reward-seeking licks were successful and contacted food (30 ± 1.6% for subject M, 28 ± 2.5% for subject R), as shown in Animation 1.
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from the experimental data.

claim: The capture rate is defined as the sum of rewards acquired, minus efforts expended, divided by time.
source: We imagined that these two forms of behavior were not independent, but rather coordinated via a control policy that maximized a single utility: the sum of rewards acquired, minus efforts expended, divided by time, termed the capture rate.
evidence: The manuscript defines the theoretical framework used in the study.

claim: Ecologists have used the capture rate formulation to understand the decisions that animals make regarding how far to travel for food, what mode of travel to use, and how long to stay before moving on to another patch.
source: We chose this formulation because it presents a normative approach that ecologists have used to understand the decisions that animals make regarding how far to travel for food, what mode of travel to use, and how long to stay before moving on to another patch (Richardson and Verbeek, 1986; Stephens and Krebs, 1987; Bautista et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The nonlinearity in effort expenditure is essential to reflect the idea that following a long work period, the capture rate must be more negative than following a short work period.
source: This nonlinearity is essential to reflect the idea that following a long work period, the capture rate must be more negative than following a short work period (i.e., more work trials produce a greater reduction in utility).
evidence: This is a theoretical justification for the model formulation.

claim: The energetic cost of reaching and the energetic cost of walking are both concave upward functions of the movement's duration.
source: Fortunately, other movements provide a clue: the energetic cost of reaching (Shadmehr et al., 2016; Huang and Ahmed, 2014) and the energetic cost of walking (Ralston, 1958; Bastien et al., 2005) are both concave upward functions of the movement's duration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: From an energetic standpoint, there is a reach speed and a walking speed that minimize the cost of each type of movement.
source: That is, from an energetic standpoint, there is a reach speed and a walking speed that minimize the cost of each type of movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited research about movement energetics.

claim: As the harvest becomes more effortful, the subject should work longer to stockpile food, but move slower to save energy.
source: Thus, as the harvest becomes more effortful, the subject should work longer to stockpile food, but move slower to save energy.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: If the subject is hungry, that is, the reward is more valuable, then they should work longer before initiating harvest.
source: In theory, this is possible: if the subject is hungry (darker lines in Figure 2C and D), that is, the reward is more valuable, then they should again work longer before initiating harvest.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the model and illustrated in Figure 2C and D.

claim: If the subject is hungry, they should move faster.
source: Paradoxically, they should also move faster.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: In response to an increased cost of harvest, one should work longer, but move with reduced vigor.
source: In summary, if decisions and actions are coordinated via a policy that aims to maximize the capture rate, then in response to an increased cost of harvest, one should work longer, but move with reduced vigor.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: In response to an increased reward value, as in hunger, one should work longer, but now move with increased vigor.
source: In response to an increased reward value, as in hunger, one should also work longer, but now move with increased vigor.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: When the tube was placed farther, marmosets attempted more trials during each work period.
source: Varying tube distance affected the decisions of the subjects: when the tube was placed farther, they chose to work longer before starting harvest (Figure 3A, left subplot): they attempted more trials during each work period (ANOVA, subject M: F(2,7908) = 41.5, p=5.2 × 10–25, subject R: F(2,10948) = 88.2, p=7 × 10–50) and produced more successful trials per work period (ANOVA, subject M: F(2,7908) = 63, p=2.8 × 10–24, subject R: F(2,10948) = 163, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3A.

claim: When the tube was placed farther, marmosets produced more successful trials per work period.
source: Varying tube distance affected the decisions of the subjects: when the tube was placed farther, they chose to work longer before starting harvest (Figure 3A, left subplot): they attempted more trials during each work period (ANOVA, subject M: F(2,7908) = 41.5, p=5.2 × 10–25, subject R: F(2,10948) = 88.2, p=7 × 10–50) and produced more successful trials per work period (ANOVA, subject M: F(2,7908) = 63, p=2.8 × 10–24, subject R: F(2,10948) = 163, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3A.

claim: The policy of delayed gratification was present throughout the recording session.
source: This policy of delayed gratification was present throughout the recording session (Figure 3A, middle plot).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from the experimental data and references Figure 3A.

claim: When the harvest required more effort, the subjects worked longer to stockpile more food before initiating their harvest.
source: That is, when the harvest required more effort, the subjects worked longer to stockpile more food before initiating their harvest (Figure 3A, right plot, effect of tube distance on food cached: subject M: F(2,9566) = 176, p<10–50, subject R: F(2,8907) = 204, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3A.

claim: Reward-relevant saccades were more vigorous than other saccades.
source: As expected, the reward-relevant saccades, that is, saccades made to visual targets (primary, corrective, and center saccades), were more vigorous than other saccades (Figure 3B, two-way ANOVA, effect of saccade type, subject M: F(1,391459) = 7,248, p<10–50, subject R: F(1,355839) = 13,641, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3B.

claim: As a work period began, the reward-relevant saccades exhibited high vigor, but then trial-by-trial, this vigor declined, reaching a low vigor value just before the work period ended.
source: As a work period began, the reward-relevant saccades exhibited high vigor, but then trial-by-trial, this vigor declined, reaching a low vigor value just before the work period ended (Figure 3C vigor).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from the experimental data and references Figure 3C.

claim: On days in which the tube was placed farther, saccade vigor was lower.
source: Remarkably, on days in which the tube was placed farther, saccade vigor was lower (RMANOVA, effect of tube distance, subject M: F(2,59033) = 224, p<10–50, subject R: F(2,50103) = 75.51, p=1.8 × 10–33).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Increasing the effort cost of extracting food during the harvest period reduced saccade vigor during the work period.
source: Thus, increasing the effort cost of extracting food during the harvest period reduced saccade vigor during the work period.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: As saccade vigor increased, both the magnitude and the variance of the endpoint error decreased.
source: However, we observed the opposite tendency: as saccade vigor increased, both the magnitude and the variance of the endpoint error decreased (Figure 3C, two-way ANOVA, effect of vigor on error magnitude, subject M: F(8,59046) = 480, p<10–50, subject R: F(8,50184) = 252, p<10–50, effect of vigor on error variance, subject M: F(8,2673) = 18,200, p<10–50, subject R: F(8,2673) = 4170, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3C.

claim: Reducing the effort costs of harvest not only promoted vigor, it also facilitated accuracy.
source: That is, reducing the effort costs of harvest not only promoted vigor, it also facilitated accuracy (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings with a citation to related work.

claim: Cognitive signals such as effort and reward are associated with changes in pupil size.
source: Cognitive signals such as effort and reward are associated with changes in pupil size (Joshi and Gold, 2020), as well as transient activation of brainstem neuromodulatory circuits in locus coeruleus (Bornert and Bouret, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cognitive signals such as effort and reward are associated with transient activation of brainstem neuromodulatory circuits in locus coeruleus.
source: Cognitive signals such as effort and reward are associated with changes in pupil size (Joshi and Gold, 2020), as well as transient activation of brainstem neuromodulatory circuits in locus coeruleus (Bornert and Bouret, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: At the onset of each work period, the pupils were dilated, but as the subjects performed more trials, the pupils constricted, exhibiting a trial-by-trial reduction that paralleled the changes in saccade vigor.
source: At the onset of each work period, the pupils were dilated, but as the subjects performed more trials, the pupils constricted, exhibiting a trial-by-trial reduction that paralleled the changes in saccade vigor (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from the experimental data and references Figure 3C.

claim: During the work period, the pupils were more dilated if the tube was placed closer to the mouth.
source: Notably, the effort cost of harvest affected pupil size: during the work period, the pupils were more dilated if the tube was placed closer to the mouth (Figure 3C, RMANOVA, effect of tube distance, subject M: F(2,60502) = 20, p=2 × 10–9, subject R: F(2,50431) = 23.8, p=4.9 × 10–11).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3C.

claim: When the effort cost of harvest was lower, the pupils dilated, and the saccades were invigorated.
source: That is, when the effort cost of harvest was lower, the pupils dilated, and the saccades were invigorated.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: When we increased the effort cost of harvest, the pupils constricted and the movements slowed, but subjects chose to work more trials before initiating harvest.
source: In summary, when we increased the effort cost of harvest, both the movements and the decisions changed: the pupils constricted and the movements slowed, but they chose to work more trials before initiating harvest.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: As amplitude increased, lick peak velocity increased during both protraction and retraction.
source: As amplitude increased, lick peak velocity increased during both protraction and retraction (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from the experimental data and references Figure 4A.

claim: Reward-seeking licks were more vigorous than grooming licks.
source: Reward-seeking licks were more vigorous than grooming licks (two-way ANOVA, effect of lick type, protraction, subject M: F(1,272233) = 66, p=4.5 × 10–16, subject R: F(1,229052) = 698, p<10–50), and retraction was more vigorous than protraction (reward-seeking licks, retraction vs. protraction, subject M: t(241145) = 532, p<10–50, subject R: t(213674) = 665, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Retraction was more vigorous than protraction for reward-seeking licks.
source: Reward-seeking licks were more vigorous than grooming licks (two-way ANOVA, effect of lick type, protraction, subject M: F(1,272233) = 66, p=4.5 × 10–16, subject R: F(1,229052) = 698, p<10–50), and retraction was more vigorous than protraction (reward-seeking licks, retraction vs. protraction, subject M: t(241145) = 532, p<10–50, subject R: t(213674) = 665, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: As the harvest began, the first lick was very low vigor, but lick after lick, the movements gathered velocity, reaching peak vigor by the third or the fourth lick.
source: As the harvest began, the first lick was very low vigor, but lick after lick, the movements gathered velocity, reaching peak vigor by the third or the fourth lick (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from the experimental data and references Figure 4B.

claim: As the harvest continued, lick vigor gradually declined.
source: As the harvest continued, lick vigor gradually declined.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from the experimental data.

claim: Licks had a lower vigor in sessions in which the tube was placed farther from the mouth.
source: Like saccades, licks had a lower vigor in sessions in which the tube was placed farther from the mouth (RMANOVA, effect of tube distance, subject M: F(2,59033) = 222.5, p<10–50, subject R: F(2,133502) = 224, p<10–50), and this pattern was present during the entire recording session (Figure 4C, left subplot).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4C.

claim: An increased effort cost of harvest promoted sloth: reduced vigor of saccades during the work period and reduced vigor of licks during the harvest period.
source: Thus, an increased effort cost of harvest promoted sloth: reduced vigor of saccades during the work period and reduced vigor of licks during the harvest period.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: During licking, the pupil size changed with a pattern that closely paralleled lick vigor: as the harvest began, pupil size was small, but it rapidly increased during the early licks, then gradually declined as the harvest continued.
source: During licking, the pupil size changed with a pattern that closely paralleled lick vigor: as the harvest began, pupil size was small, but it rapidly increased during the early licks, then gradually declined as the harvest continued (Figure 4B, right subplot).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from the experimental data and references Figure 4B.

claim: The pupils were more dilated in sessions in which the tube was closer to the mouth.
source: Importantly, the pupils were more dilated in sessions in which the tube was closer to the mouth (Figure 4C, right subplot, effect of tube distance, subject M: F(2,166742) = 583, p<10–50, subject R: F(2,130493) = 118, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4C.

claim: When the effort cost of reward increased, the pupils constricted, and the vigor of both saccades and licks decreased.
source: As a result, when the effort cost of reward increased, the pupils constricted, and the vigor of both saccades and licks decreased.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Within a harvest period, lick vigor rapidly increased and then gradually declined.
source: In summary, within a harvest period, lick vigor rapidly increased and then gradually declined.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Simultaneous with the changes in vigor, the pupils rapidly dilated and then gradually constricted.
source: Simultaneous with the changes in vigor, the pupils rapidly dilated and then gradually constricted.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: In sessions where the tube was placed farther from the mouth, the licks had lower vigor and the pupils were more constricted.
source: In sessions where the tube was placed farther from the mouth, the licks had lower vigor and the pupils were more constricted.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: When the work period had included many completed trials, then the movements in the ensuing harvest period were more vigorous.
source: We found that when the work period had included many completed trials, then the movements in the ensuing harvest period were more vigorous (Figure 4D, two-way ANOVA, effect of trials, subject M: F(4, 164242) = 353, p<10–50, subject R: F(4,123411) = 152, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4D.

claim: The licks were invigorated by the amount of food that awaited harvest.
source: Thus, the licks were invigorated by the amount of food that awaited harvest.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Following a successful lick, there was a large increase in lick vigor.
source: Following a successful lick, there was a large increase in lick vigor (Figure 4E, subject M: t(85182) = 40, p<10–50, subject R: t(81378) = 104, p<10–50), and a large increase in pupil size (subject M: F(84969) = 57, p<10–50, subject R: t(80318) = 94, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4E.

claim: Following a successful lick, there was a large increase in pupil size.
source: Following a successful lick, there was a large increase in lick vigor (Figure 4E, subject M: t(85182) = 40, p<10–50, subject R: t(81378) = 104, p<10–50), and a large increase in pupil size (subject M: F(84969) = 57, p<10–50, subject R: t(80318) = 94, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4E.

claim: Following a failed lick the subjects either reduced or did not increase their lick vigor.
source: In contrast, following a failed lick the subjects either reduced or did not increase their lick vigor (Figure 4E, subject M: t(114159) = 0.88, p=0.37, subject R: t(97164) = -44, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4E.

claim: Following a failed lick, there was a smaller increase in pupil size compared to a successful lick.
source: This failure also produced a smaller increase in pupil size (comparison to successful lick, two-sample t-test, subject M: t(198722) = 14.8, p=4.3 × 10–50, subject R: t(176044) = 53, p<10–50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: A single successful lick led to acquisition of reward, which then was followed by a relatively large increase in pupil size, and an invigorated subsequent lick.
source: Thus, a single successful lick led to acquisition of reward, which then was followed by a relatively large increase in pupil size, and an invigorated subsequent lick.
